evidence.finding: Routing version 24.7 was deployed to all queues at 09:15, exactly matching incident onset.
Transfer rates increased 87.6%–116.9% across all four queues after the deployment.
AHT increased approximately 35%–38% in every queue after incident onset.
Mean service level declined from 80.8% before onset to 61.0% afterward, while ASA increased 67.5%.
Scheduled and logged-in staffing remained constant at 49; productive staffing was essentially unchanged.
Mean offered calls decreased 6.1% after onset, contradicting a demand spike.

primary_root_cause_detail: Routing configuration version 24.7 was deployed across all queues at 09:15, coinciding exactly with the incident onset. Transfer rates then increased 87.6%–116.9% and AHT increased approximately 35%–38% across queues, reducing throughput and degrading service level despite stable staffing and no demand surge.
recommended_actions: Rollback or correct routing configuration version 24.7 and validate skill-to-queue mappings.
Monitor transfer rate, AHT, ASA, and service level by queue immediately after remediation.
Add pre-deployment regression checks for routing paths, transfer loops, and queue assignments.
Establish automated post-deployment alerts for abrupt cross-queue transfer-rate and AHT increases.

rejected_hypotheses.reason: Aggregate offered calls decreased after onset, and three of four queues had lower volume.
Scheduled and logged-in staffing remained constant, with no material productive-headcount loss.
No platform event was recorded; the only visible operational event was the routing deployment.
Service level recalculated exactly for all 16 intervals, with zero material mismatch.

stakeholder_summary: The service-level decline was most likely caused by the 09:15 routing deployment. The change coincided with roughly doubled transfer rates and a 35%–38% AHT increase across queues, reducing throughput. Demand and staffing were stable, and reported service-level calculations were valid.
